findings.title: projen majorVersion is 1 but the package has only ever published 0.x (latest 0.3.8)
findings.detail: RootConfig.ts sets majorVersion: 1 and prerelease: 'alpha', yet npm shows 50 published versions all in 0.x with no 1.x, no alpha, and only a 'latest' dist-tag. The config has never produced a shipped release. To make the v3 redesign version 1.0.0-alpha (decision D6), main's majorVersion must move to 0 to avoid a release-branch major collision — which also aligns the config with the actually-published 0.x line. Confirm the maintainer's intent for the current line before changing main's release config or enabling the v3 release branch.

findings.title: The asciinema-recorder skill only documents interactive shell-wrapping, not the scripted recording + mp4 export this repo's milestone proofs need
findings.detail: Decision D3 says to build the milestone recorder on the user's asciinema-recorder skill. The skill's actual workflow is 'exit your agent, wrap your shell in asciinema rec, work normally' and it assumes brew/apt for installation. A milestone gate has to produce its proof unattended, so test/proof/record-demo.sh uses 'asciinema rec --command <script>' instead, and the skill documents no cast->mp4 export path at all (no agg/ffmpeg). The recorder built here works and is self-contained, so nothing is blocked. Out of scope to fix because the skill lives outside this repo in a shared global skills directory and editing it would change behaviour for the user's other projects; the skill's own self-evolution policy would have it patched, so raise it with the maintainer rather than silently amending a shared file.

findings.title: npx projen compat is already failing with 64 pre-existing API-removal errors, so it cannot serve as the API-break tripwire
findings.detail: CLAUDE.md names 'npx projen compat' as the tripwire that guards the published multi-language API, and ground rule 1 relies on it. It currently exits 1 with 64 'has been removed' errors before any v3 work is added, so it reports nothing useful. Root cause looks like aws-cdk-lib version skew rather than a deliberate API change: the removals are overwhelmingly members this repo inherits from aws-cdk-lib rather than declares (propertyInjectors on many *Props structs, Stack.removeStackTag, Stack.env, and the .with() methods on IEncryptionKey/IParameterConstruct/IRepositoryStack). The dependency is declared as a caret range (aws-cdk-lib@^<cdkVersion>) while the lockfile resolves locally to exactly the range floor, so the published release was compiled against a newer minor that has those members and the local build is compared against an older one that does not. Confirmed unrelated to the v3 work: 0 of the 122 types in the generated .jsii assembly are sourced from src/v3, so the new module contributes nothing to the diff. Left unfixed because resolving it means moving a dependency version or curating a .compatignore (which does not exist yet) for the published 0.x line, both outside an additive v3 task. Consequence while it stays red: a genuine break in the v3 public surface introduced by m1-accessor or a later milestone would be indistinguishable from this noise, so treat compat as uninformative until it is fixed. Fix direction: align the resolved aws-cdk-lib with the version the last release was built against, re-diff, and only then add genuinely-accepted keys to a .compatignore.

findings.title: Exported bare functions compile fine but are silently dropped from the jsii assembly, so they do not exist for Python/Java/.NET consumers
findings.detail: jsii only models types, so a bare exported function is compiled by tsc and then omitted from the generated assembly with no error and no warning. Verified against the existing published surface: mergeCodeBuildOptions is exported from the package entry point via src/resource-providers, yet the generated .jsii contains zero entries for it. TypeScript consumers can call it; Python, Java and .NET consumers cannot see it at all. This is pre-existing on the current 0.x line, not introduced by v3, and it is a silent failure mode rather than a build break, which is why it has gone unnoticed. Recorded here because it is a trap for every future milestone: the v3 public barrel deliberately exports only classes, interfaces and enums for this reason, and anything that needs to be callable from a non-TS language has to be a static method on a class rather than a function. Fix direction for the existing case: decide whether mergeCodeBuildOptions is meant to be public, and if so move it onto a class; if not, stop exporting it from the entry point.

findings.title: applyDerivedDefaults silently discards an aws value that is present but not an object, repairing a typo from ambient env instead of reporting it
findings.detail: applyDerivedDefaults replaces a non-plain-object aws value with a fresh object and then fills it from the environment, so a config file that says aws as a bare string or a list has that value thrown away with no signal. If the caller's schema lists aws.accountId as a required key the mistake still fails closed with MISSING_KEY, but if it does not, the typo is silently repaired from CDK_DEFAULT_ACCOUNT/CDK_DEFAULT_REGION and the user never learns their config was ignored. Consistent with the deliberate, tested behaviour that a whole config document which is not an object falls back to base defaults, so it is not an inconsistency so much as an open design question. Left unfixed because reporting it honestly needs a fifth ConfigError kind for a type mismatch, and the m1-validation task scope is explicitly ConfigError with four kinds. Revisit when M3 resolves config for real stages, where a silently ignored aws block would be much more costly.

findings.title: The level0-app fixture omits the cdk.json context feature-flag block that real cdk init emits, so it synthesizes under legacy defaults
findings.detail: level0-app exists to prove Level-0 inertness against an untouched cdk init app, and its TypeScript is faithful: it imports only aws-cdk-lib and constructs, with no wrapper symbol anywhere. Its cdk.json, however, is three lines, whereas cdk init app --language typescript emits a large context block of feature flags (and also package.json, jest.config.js, test/ and a watch key). The fixture therefore synthesizes under default/legacy feature-flag behaviour rather than the behaviour a newly initialised user app actually gets. Harmless for the current deploy/assert/destroy lifecycle test, which only checks a stack and an SSM parameter. It becomes a silent divergence for any later milestone that compares a synthesized template against what a real user app would produce, which is exactly what the M2 injection and M3 deploy-time-synth gates do. Fix direction: paste the feature-flag context from a real cdk init of the pinned aws-cdk version, and note the version it came from so it can be refreshed deliberately. The absent package.json is a separate, deliberate choice (root node_modules resolution) and is not part of this finding.

findings.title: The orphan sweep's stack-age arithmetic depends on GNU date and aborts the whole sweep if a timestamp fails to parse
findings.detail: cmd_sweep computes each stack's age with an arithmetic expression that embeds a date -u -d command substitution. The -d flag is GNU-specific, which is fine for this repo's Linux target but would break on BSD/macOS. More to the point, if that substitution ever produces empty output the arithmetic becomes a syntax error and the sweep exits non-zero having listed nothing useful, which is a poor failure mode for the one command whose job is finding leaked stacks. Latent rather than live: CloudFormation always returns a parseable ISO 8601 CreationTime, so there is no known input that triggers it today. Left unfixed as it is cosmetic against the reviewed change and the sweep's safety properties do not depend on the age column at all -- age is display-only and never feeds the teardown guard. Fix direction: compute the age in a guarded step and fall back to printing the raw timestamp when parsing fails.

findings.title: AppConfig.of applies base + derived defaults on the file path but not on the injected-context path, so the same app can see differently-shaped config
findings.detail: AppConfig.load (the file path) does deepMerge(getDefaultConfig(), file) then applyDerivedDefaults then validate. AppConfig.of on the injected-context path validates the raw context object with no base-defaults merge and no derived-defaults step. So an app run under the future 'cdk-cicd exec' (config arriving via cicd:config context) can see config lacking the removalPolicies RETAIN defaults and lacking CDK_DEFAULT_ACCOUNT/_REGION derivation, while the same app under plain cdk deploy (config from file) sees them. This is only correct if the injecting wrapper pre-applies base+derived defaults before writing the context value, which is what accessor.ts's comment assumes. It is latent, not a present bug, because the injecting wrapper does not exist yet. Recorded so the M2 runtime-injection milestone (m2-register and friends) does not silently reintroduce the asymmetry: either the wrapper must resolve the full config (base + derived) before writing context, or AppConfig.of must run the same merge/derive pipeline on the context value that load runs on the file. Decide which at M2 and add a test that the two paths produce identical config for identical input.

findings.title: deepMerge assigns array-valued override keys by reference, so a later mutation of the parsed config would leak into an already-merged config
findings.detail: mergeRecords recurses into plain objects (which both clones and applies the UNSAFE_KEYS filter at depth) but assigns any non-plain-object value, including arrays, directly: result[key] = value. The deepMerge doc correctly says arrays replace rather than concatenate, and that is the intended semantics, but it does not clone them. The 'override object is not aliased into the result' test covers nested objects only, not arrays, so an array-valued key in the merged result is the same reference as in the caller's parsed object. Harmless today because the loader does not mutate the parsed config after merging and callers are not expected to either. It would become a real aliasing bug if any later code mutates a parsed config in place after AppConfig has returned. Fix direction if revisited: shallow-copy arrays on assignment (result[key] = value.slice() when Array.isArray(value)) and extend the aliasing test to an array-valued key.

findings.title: FieldKind.STRING_LIST validation checks only that the value is a non-empty array, not that its elements are strings
findings.detail: isMissing for STRING_LIST returns false as soon as the value is an array with length > 0, so a config value like [1, 2] or a mixed list satisfies a field declared STRING_LIST. This matches the enum member's documented semantics ('A non-empty array'), so it is very likely intentional rather than a defect, and tightening it would be a behaviour change that could reject configs that validate today. Recorded only so the choice stays conscious: if a later milestone relies on STRING_LIST fields actually being lists of strings (e.g. availabilityZones passed straight into a CDK construct that will throw on a non-string), either strengthen isMissing to check every element is a non-blank string or rename the kind to make the loose semantics explicit. No change now.

findings.title: The preload's construction-time config read sees a narrower context set than AppConfig.of, so a cicd:config in cdk.json drives the read side but not the injected tags/synthesizer
findings.detail: register.ts's readInjectedConfig runs before super(), when there is no App node, so it can only consult props.context and CDK_CONTEXT_JSON. The read side, AppConfig.of, reads the App's fully-merged context and its docstring notes cicd:config can also be hand-set in cdk.json's context field. So a cicd:config placed directly in cdk.json would be seen by AppConfig.of (used inside stacks) but would NOT drive the hook's tags/synthesizer, because the hook cannot read the cdk.json file pre-super without a node. This is fine for the supported path -- cdk-cicd exec (m2-exec) injects via CDK_CONTEXT_JSON, and command-line --context is merged into CDK_CONTEXT_JSON by the CDK CLI, so both are covered. It is an asymmetry to keep in mind when m2-exec is built and when documenting how config reaches the wrapper: the hook's inputs are CDK_CONTEXT_JSON + AppProps.context only. Fix direction if it ever bites: have exec normalise a cdk.json-level cicd:config into CDK_CONTEXT_JSON, or document that cdk.json-level cicd:config is read-only (consumed by AppConfig.of, not by injection).

findings.title: The multi-copy App patch does not check that the distinct aws-cdk-lib copies agree on version, so a dev/monorepo minor-version skew could silently misapply Aspects/tags
findings.detail: register.ts patches every distinct aws-cdk-lib copy reachable from the app entry / cwd / the hook, to survive workspaces that carry more than one copy. The cross-copy mechanism is sound for SAME-version copies: Aspects.of stores under Symbol.for('cdk-aspects') (a hardcoded global-registry key) and synthesis reads it back the same way, so the nested-copy applyWrapper and the root-copy synth share the same node metadata slot regardless of which copy's class created the App. All copies in this workspace are 2.195.0. The latent fragility: if two copies disagree on aws-cdk-lib minor version, data written by one copy's classes is read by another's synth logic, and interface drift (e.g. aspect-priority handling) could silently misbehave. Published installs are single-copy because aws-cdk-lib is a peerDependency, so this never affects users -- only dev/monorepo setups. Optional hardening: have distinctCdkCopies emit a warning (not throw) when the resolved copies' versions differ, so a skew is visible rather than silent. Not a correctness bug at the pinned version.

findings.title: CdkCicd.attach reuses markAppConstructed(), conflating an explicit attach with a wrapped-constructor App -- fine for today's diagnostic, revisit when m2-bundled-diagnostic is built
findings.detail: The construction counter (inject.ts markAppConstructed/appsConstructed) is named for Apps that pass through the wrapped constructor, but CdkCicd.attach also increments it so that an app which opts into attach counts as wrapped and the future bundled-app diagnostic stays silent. The counter's real semantic (appsConstructed = 'Apps the wrapper has wrapped') is satisfied and this is correct for the diagnostic's only current requirement (non-zero when the wrapper was applied). The coupling is baked in before m2-bundled-diagnostic exists: if that diagnostic later needs to distinguish an attach from constructor-wrapping (e.g. to warn that a non-bundled app called attach unnecessarily), this shared counter is too coarse and attach would need its own signal. Resolve when building m2-bundled-diagnostic: either keep the shared counter (if 'was the wrapper applied at all' stays the only question) or split into distinct construct-vs-attach counters. No change needed now.

findings.title: The CDK_CICD_EXEC arming flag is a cross-package contract exported only from an internal deep path, so m2-exec will likely duplicate the literal string
findings.detail: The bundled-app diagnostic arms only when process.env.CDK_CICD_EXEC === '1'. That flag is defined as EXEC_FLAG in the wrapper's internal src/v3/runtime/inject.ts, but its OTHER end -- the cdk-cicd exec launcher -- lives in the separate cdk-cicd-wrapper-cli package, which cannot import a non-exported deep runtime path (the jsii package's exports map does not publish it, and importing lib/v3/runtime/inject reaches past the public surface). So m2-exec will most likely hardcode the literal 'CDK_CICD_EXEC' a second time. Resolve when building m2-exec: either expose the flag name somewhere the CLI can import cleanly, or add a small test that asserts the two copies of the string agree, so a rename on one side cannot silently disarm the diagnostic on real runs.

findings.title: The bundled-diagnostic subprocess test depends on a compiled lib/ that the test task does not build, so it only passes after a separate compile step
findings.detail: bundled-diagnostic.test.ts runs the COMPILED preload (lib/v3/runtime/register.js) under node -r in a subprocess -- the only faithful way to exercise a process.on('exit') handler. But the projen 'test' task is jest + eslint with no compile step, and lib/ is gitignored, so a bare `npx jest` after a clean checkout would hit the test's beforeAll guard ('run npx projen compile first') and fail deterministically. It passes under the canonical `npm run build` (compile then test) and in this session because compile was run first. Not flaky, just order-dependent. Fix direction: have the wrapper's projen 'test' task spawn 'compile' first, or move the subprocess wiring test behind an integration-test task that depends on compile, so the standalone `npx jest` invocation is self-sufficient.

findings.title: The CLI's yargs usage breaks on yargs 18, which floated in on a projen regen and broke the entire CLI until yargs was pinned to ^17
findings.detail: src/index.ts does `import * as yargs from 'yargs'; const ya = yargs; ya.command(...)`. That namespace-as-instance pattern is a yargs v17 idiom; yargs 18 (released recently) changed its exports and `ya.command` is no longer a function, so `node lib/index.js` throws 'ya.command is not a function' and every CLI subcommand fails. This surfaced when enabling the wrapper dependency for m2-exec required a `npx projen` regen, which re-resolved the previously-unpinned `yargs` dep from 17.7.3 up to 18.0.0. Worked around by pinning `yargs@^17.7.3` + `@types/yargs@^17.0.33` in projenrc/CLIConfig.ts, which restores the working CLI and is the surgical fix. The real follow-up is to migrate the CLI's yargs bootstrap to the v18 API (call the factory / default import instead of the namespace) and then unpin, so the CLI can take yargs security updates. Out of scope for m2-exec, which only needed the CLI to run.

findings.title: level1-app/cicd.config.ts still carries a 'NOT ACTIVE YET -- defineCICD/Repository do not exist until wave 3' header, which is now false
findings.detail: As of m3-definecicd, defineCICD and Repository exist and the fixture's cicd.config.ts loads and normalizes via ts-node. Its header comment (lines ~4-8) still says the symbols do not exist until wave 3 and that the file is dormant, and the file is still listed in the fixture's tsconfig.json exclude. Left unchanged by the m3-definecicd unit on purpose (surgical scope): the file belongs to m3-config-discovery, which is the task that actually wires discovery/loading and should update the header (and decide whether to drop the tsconfig exclude) as part of activating it. Resolve when implementing m3-config-discovery: refresh the header to describe how the CLI discovers and loads the file, and remove the now-misleading 'not active' language.

findings.title: ts-node is required to load a .ts cicd.config (and by exec's -r ts-node/register) but is not a declared CLI dependency, so a global install can fail to resolve it
findings.detail: CicdConfig.load does an in-process require('ts-node/register') for a .ts config, and ExecCommand spawns node with -r ts-node/register for a .ts entry. ts-node resolves today only because it is hoisted into the workspace-root node_modules; it is NOT in the CLI package's dependencies. For a locally-installed CLI, in-process resolution walks up into the user's project and usually finds their ts-node; but a GLOBALLY-installed CLI (npm i -g) does not, so a user with a TypeScript cicd.config.ts (or a .ts app entry under exec) hits a module-resolution failure. Mitigated now: CicdConfig.load wraps the require in a clear, actionable error ('needs ts-node ... install it or compile to cicd.config.js') instead of a raw crash; the .ts path is unit-covered. The real fix is a distribution decision to make deliberately before external publish: declare ts-node as a CLI dependency in projenrc/CLIConfig.ts (pin the version to avoid a yargs-18-style float on regen), and apply the same clear-error treatment to the exec spawn path. Out of scope for m3-config-discovery's minimal change; track for the publish/harness-publish-loop work.

findings.title: resolveEnvTarget's cicd-config stage tier never fires on a live `cdk deploy` because the CDK CLI always pre-sets CDK_DEFAULT_ACCOUNT/REGION, which win by precedence
findings.detail: resolveEnvTarget precedence is (already-set CDK_DEFAULT_* > matching cicd.config stage > app-config aws.*). On a live `cdk deploy`/`cdk synth` the CDK CLI pre-sets CDK_DEFAULT_REGION (from AWS_REGION/profile) and CDK_DEFAULT_ACCOUNT (from resolved STS creds) before running the app command, so the env tier always wins and the cicd-config stage tier is effectively dead on the direct-CLI path -- a `CDK_STAGE=dev cdk deploy` uses the ambient region/account, not the cicd.config dev stage's. This is intended: the real deploy path is `cdk-cicd synth` -> per-region assembly (which sets AWS_REGION to steer the CLI) -> `cdk-cicd deploy`, with account/region correctness enforced by m3-drift-check, not by exec. The cicd-stage tier still matters for a bare `node -r register app.js` (no CDK CLI) or a future path where CDK_DEFAULT_* is genuinely unset. Recorded so the precedence is not mistaken for driving the live target. No change needed; revisit if the direct-CLI path should honor cicd.config stage env (it would need AWS_REGION steering like synth does).

findings.title: cdk-cicd synth pins CDK_DEFAULT_ACCOUNT per target but the CDK CLI re-derives account from STS, so (unlike region via AWS_REGION) the account pin is cosmetic
findings.detail: synthTargets sets AWS_REGION/AWS_DEFAULT_REGION to steer the CLI's per-region synth, which works because the CLI derives the app's CDK_DEFAULT_REGION from AWS_REGION. It also sets CDK_DEFAULT_ACCOUNT/CDK_DEPLOY_ACCOUNT from the stage, but there is no AWS_* account analogue: the CDK CLI re-derives CDK_DEFAULT_ACCOUNT from the resolved STS identity and overrides the pin, so a stage account that differs from the ambient creds does NOT change the synthesized account -- the account pin is cosmetic during synth. Harmless for the single-account sandbox, and catching an account that disagrees with the deploy target is exactly m3-drift-check's job (it reads the synthesized manifest's aws://account/region). Recorded as the region/account asymmetry so a future multi-account synth path knows the account cannot be steered the same way region is (it needs assumed creds for the target account, not just an env var).

findings.title: DriftCheck skips the account guard when DriftTarget.account is undefined, so m3-deploy MUST pass the STS-resolved deploy account or the abort is bypassable
findings.detail: analyzeManifest, by documented design, skips the account-mismatch check when target.account is undefined (account omitted = 'whatever the creds resolve'). That is fine for the m3-drift-check unit in isolation, but it is a live seam risk for m3-deploy: if deploy calls checkAssembly with a DriftTarget whose account comes from the cicd.config stage (which may be undefined, and per finding code-review-synth-account-pin-cosmetic the synth cannot force it anyway), then a manifest carrying a concrete FOREIGN account -- exactly the hardcoded-env-app shape the drift rule exists to stop -- passes as ok and would deploy. Fix belongs in m3-deploy: populate DriftTarget.account from the STS-resolved deploy-time identity (aws sts get-caller-identity / the harness account), never from the possibly-undefined stage config, so the account the deploy will actually use is the one the manifest is checked against. Recorded so m3-deploy does not reintroduce the gap.

findings.title: A partially-agnostic environment (e.g. aws://unknown-account/us-east-1) is treated as fully agnostic, dropping a region-mismatch warning
findings.detail: analyzeManifest treats a stack as agnostic when EITHER the account or the region is unknown-*. So an env like aws://unknown-account/us-east-1 (concrete but wrong region) short-circuits to 'agnostic' and never emits the region-mismatch warning it otherwise would. Impact is only a lost WARNING (never a blocked deploy -- account is unknown so the account guard correctly does not fire either), and this mixed shape is unusual in real CDK output (an env-agnostic stack is normally unknown-account AND unknown-region). Left as-is for simplicity. Revisit only if a real assembly is observed producing the mixed shape and the missing region warning matters; the fix is to evaluate account-agnostic and region-agnostic independently.

findings.title: m3-forced-roles sets the deploy and CFN-execution roles but leaves asset-publishing/lookup roles at bootstrap defaults
findings.detail: resolveSynthesizer threads CDK_CICD_DEPLOY_ROLE_ARN and CDK_CICD_CFN_EXEC_ROLE_ARN into DefaultStackSynthesizer, but the asset file/image publishing roles and the lookup role keep their bootstrap defaults. In a strict setup where the default asset roles are unusable (e.g. a locked-down bootstrap), assets would still publish under bootstrap roles while the stack deploys under the forced role -- a partial forcing. This is the documented M3 scope: the design (v3-devops-experience.md ~214-218) leaves full synthesizer control (all roles baked into the manifest) to a later escape hatch, and app-staging's DeploymentIdentities.specifyRoles is deferred (alpha). Recorded so it is not rediscovered as a bug when the full-control escape hatch lands: extend resolveSynthesizer to also accept fileAssetPublishingRoleArn/imageAssetPublishingRoleArn/lookupRoleArn from env (or move to AppStagingSynthesizer.DeploymentIdentities) when a consumer needs strict asset roles.

findings.title: For a stage with no deployment config, an ambient CDK_CICD_DEPLOY_ROLE_ARN/CFN_EXEC_ROLE_ARN in the caller's env is still honored by the preload
findings.detail: exec folds forcedRoleEnv(cicdStage) into childEnv after ...process.env, so a stage that configures roles overrides the ambient value (correct, stage-wins). But when the stage has NO deployment, forcedRoleEnv returns {} and any ambient CDK_CICD_DEPLOY_ROLE_ARN/CDK_CICD_CFN_EXEC_ROLE_ARN in the caller's environment passes straight through ...process.env and is read by resolveSynthesizer. These are undocumented wrapper-private contract vars, so real-world impact is nil, but the 'no deployment => no forced roles' guarantee only holds with a clean ambient environment. Optional hardening if it ever matters: have exec explicitly clear the two role vars when the resolved stage has no deployment, so the stage config is the sole source of truth regardless of ambient env.

findings.title: cdk-cicd deploy fails OPEN on the account drift guard when STS/the aws CLI cannot resolve the deploy account (drift degrades to region-only and deploy proceeds on a warning)
findings.detail: DeployCommand resolves the deploy account by spawning `aws sts get-caller-identity`. When that returns undefined -- the aws CLI is not on PATH (realistic in CI that sets AWS_* env creds and installs only node/cdk), or STS errors -- it warns and passes account:undefined to checkAssembly, which then skips the account-mismatch check entirely and deploys on region-only drift. So the very guard meant to stop a foreign/hardcoded account is silently downgraded on the STS-unavailable path (a sibling of the honored finding code-review-driftcheck-undefined-account-bypasses-guard, via a different route). Rated medium not high because the degradation is bounded: a genuinely foreign hardcoded account would still make `cdk deploy`'s own assume-role fail -- a late, ugly failure rather than a silent wrong-account deploy. Two related notes: (F3) this introduces an `aws` CLI PATH dependency that `cdk-cicd synth`/`exec` do not have. Fix direction (maintainer decision, before external publish): either FAIL CLOSED (block deploy when the account cannot be resolved), or resolve the account via @aws-sdk/client-sts (add the dep) / a documented CDK_DEPLOY_ACCOUNT env fallback, so the guard never silently downgrades and the aws-CLI dependency is removed.

findings.title: m2-injection demo would now print a cdk-cicd-wrapper-test tag its narration does not explain (only on a future re-record)
findings.detail: m3-verify added a static cdk-cicd-wrapper-test tag to level1-app/config/dev.json (so the teardown guard can destroy stacks that `cdk-cicd deploy` created without the harness's own --tags). The m2-injection demo's `marker level1 tags` step now prints {cdk-cicd-wrapper-test, Stage}, but the narration ('the Stage tag was applied tree-wide') mentions only Stage. No account-id leak (static string) and the committed mp4 is unchanged, so this bites only if/when the m2-injection demo is re-recorded. Out of scope for the m3-verify unit (touches the m2 demo script). Fix when re-recording m2-injection: either add a one-line say() explaining the harness tag, or point the demo's config read at a stage/config without the test tag.

findings.title: m3-verify assert_region_deployed reports 'not wrapped' even when the underlying get-template call itself failed
findings.detail: assert_region_deployed does `aws_masked cloudformation get-template ... | grep -q '"Stage"' || die '...lacks the injected Stage tag -- not wrapped'`. Under pipefail a get-template API failure (throttling, transient error) also trips the `|| die` and is reported as 'not wrapped' rather than the real cause. It is fail-CLOSED (correct direction for a positive assertion -- the gate errors rather than passing), so this is a message/consistency nit versus m2-verify's deliberately-split has_wrapper_tag, not a correctness bug. Fix if revisited: split the get-template call from the grep (capture, die on the AWS call failing with a distinct message, then grep the captured body) -- mirroring the m2-verify has_wrapper_tag hardening.

findings.title: The CodePipeline deploy CodeBuild project has no deploy IAM, so a real pipeline run will fail AccessDenied -- blocks m4-verify
findings.detail: CodePipelineEngine's per-stage deploy PipelineProject runs `npx cdk-cicd deploy --stage <name>`, which runs `cdk deploy` and needs sts:AssumeRole on the CDK bootstrap roles (cdk-<qualifier>-{deploy,file-publishing,image-publishing,lookup}-role-*) plus SSM read of the bootstrap version param. The engine grants the project's default CodeBuild service role none of this, so a real deploy fails with AccessDenied. Synth-level tests cannot catch it (the engine skeleton is correct at synth). No existing M4 task explicitly owns this IAM. It must be added before m4-verify's 'a commit flows dev->prod' gate can go green: grant the deploy project role assume-role on the bootstrap role ARNs, scoped to the target account/region (wherever the deploy-time role wiring lands -- likely m4-support-resources or a small addition in the engine). Recorded so m4-verify is not surprised. RESOLVED by m4-support-resources: grantDeployPermissions gives each stage's deploy project sts:AssumeRole on the four bootstrap roles for every (account, region) the stage targets, plus the stage's forced deployer role when one is configured, plus ssm:GetParameter on the bootstrap version parameter. Verified against the installed aws-cdk-lib/aws-cdk sources rather than from memory: the role-name pattern and default qualifier match DefaultStackSynthesizer, sts:AssumeRole alone is sufficient (sts:TagSession is only needed when assumeRoleAdditionalOptions sets session tags, which the wrapper never does), and a missing grant would fail loudly rather than silently. The grant carries zero wildcards -- narrower than aws-cdk-lib's own pipelines module, which uses cdk-<qualifier>-*. Two residual gaps were split into their own findings rather than left under this one: code-review-bootstrap-qualifier-not-single-source-of-truth and code-review-ci-project-lacks-lookup-role. Still to be proven end-to-end on real AWS by m4-verify.

findings.title: CodePipelineEngine adds no cdk-nag suppressions for the pipeline's own auto-generated roles/bucket -- will block pipeline-stack synth if AwsSolutionsChecks runs on it
findings.detail: v3 applies AwsSolutionsChecks on the workload app (inject.ts applyWrapper). The CodePipeline engine's auto-generated pipeline role, CodeBuild roles and artifact bucket carry wildcard IAM (IAM5) and other findings that v2 suppressed (CDKPipeline.ts:312-368). When m4-approval-selfupdate's `cdk-cicd deploy-ci` provisions the pipeline stack, if that path applies AwsSolutionsChecks, synth of the pipeline stack will error and block provisioning. Adding suppressions now is premature -- the provisioning app (PipelineApp) does not exist yet, so where they attach is unknown -- hence logged, not fixed here. m4-approval-selfupdate / m4-verify must port v2's pipeline suppression list (or decide the pipeline stack is not nag-checked). Flagged prominently so the M4 gate is not blocked by an un-suppressed nag error. Update after m4-support-resources: the surface grew slightly. The support artifact bucket has no server access logging (S1), and under removalPolicy DESTROY the stack also contains a Custom::S3AutoDeleteObjects custom resource whose provider Lambda carries a managed policy and a broad inline policy (IAM4/IAM5) and a pinned runtime (L1). That is a few more entries in the suppression list this task already has to write -- no restructuring needed, and the count is reasoned from the rendered template rather than measured with cdk-nag.

findings.title: CodePipelineEngine does not yet read stage.manualApproval (no ManualApprovalAction) -- owned by m4-approval-selfupdate
findings.detail: ResolvedStage.manualApproval is populated but the engine's render() ignores it: no codepipeline_actions.ManualApprovalAction is inserted before a gated stage's deploy action, and render returns void (no handle to the created Pipeline). This is expected for the m4-codepipeline skeleton -- real approval gates are m4-approval-selfupdate. Cleanest resolution: have the engine itself read stage.manualApproval and insert the approval action before the deploy action (no pipeline getter needed, keeping render void). Recorded as the seam m4-approval-selfupdate builds on. RESOLVED (m4-approval-selfupdate, approval half): the engine now reads `stage.manualApproval` and emits a ManualApprovalAction at runOrder 1 with the stage deploy at runOrder 2, in the SAME pipeline stage, so `render` still returns void and gating adds no pipeline stage, no CodeBuild project and no SNS topic. Verified against the rendered template and by a review pass that tried the obvious wrong implementations (approval at the same run order, approval in its own stage, approval on every stage) against the new tests.

findings.title: The bootstrap qualifier has three independent sources (config, cdk.json context, the hardcoded default) and nothing reconciles them, so a custom qualifier breaks the pipeline's deploy stage
findings.detail: Three places decide which CDK bootstrap roles matter and they can disagree. (1) ResolvedCicdConfig.qualifier is documented as 'drives the bootstrap qualifier and asset naming' but is read by nothing: resolveSynthesizer (v3/runtime/inject.ts) builds a plain DefaultStackSynthesizer and never threads it. (2) A user's own cdk.json may set the @aws-cdk/core:bootstrapQualifier context, which DefaultStackSynthesizer.bind DOES honour (BOOTSTRAP_QUALIFIER_CONTEXT), so their app's manifest names cdk-<theirQualifier>-*-role-* roles. (3) The engine's grantDeployPermissions hardcodes DefaultStackSynthesizer.DEFAULT_QUALIFIER when building the assume-role grant, because keying it off config.qualifier would point at roles that do not exist while (1) holds. Live consequence today: a user with a custom-qualifier bootstrap sets the context, their app asks to assume cdk-<theirQualifier>-deploy-role-*, the deploy CodeBuild role may only assume the default-qualifier roles, and the deploy stage dies with 'Could not assume role in target account'. Latent consequence: whoever fixes (1) by threading config.qualifier into the synthesizer silently breaks the IAM in (3), and no test catches it because the engine test asserts the default qualifier literally. Fix direction: make ONE resolved qualifier the single source of truth -- resolve it once (config.qualifier, else the app's bootstrapQualifier context, else the default), thread it to both the synthesizer and the engine's IAM, and add a test that a non-default qualifier moves both together.

findings.title: The CI/Build CodeBuild project runs cdk synth but gets no bootstrap lookup-role grant, so a workload using context lookups fails at the Build stage
findings.detail: m4-support-resources grants bootstrap assume-role only to the per-stage Deploy projects; the Build project (which runs `cdk-cicd synth --all`) gets nothing. cdk synth resolves context providers -- Vpc.fromLookup, HostedZone.fromLookup, AMI lookups and friends -- by assuming the bootstrap lookup role, so a workload that uses any of them fails at the Build stage before a deploy stage ever runs. Not a blocker for the M4 gate, whose fixture is a trivial app with no lookups, so it is invisible to m4-verify; it is a v2-parity functional gap on a user-visible path. Note the same gap does not apply to deploy-time synth: the Deploy projects do get the lookup role. Fix direction: grant the Build project sts:AssumeRole on the lookup role for every (account, region) any stage targets -- ideally sharing one resolved account/region set with grantDeployPermissions rather than duplicating the ARN construction.

findings.title: The deploy project is granted the image-publishing bootstrap role but runs unprivileged with no Docker daemon, so a workload with a container asset still cannot deploy
findings.detail: grantDeployPermissions includes the image-publishing bootstrap role in the assume-role grant, which implies the pipeline can publish container assets. It cannot: PipelineProject defaults to privileged: false and the engine sets no override, so there is no Docker daemon in the build container and a workload with a DockerImageAsset (or a bundled Lambda that shells out to Docker) fails during cdk deploy regardless of IAM. v2 handled this by running its synth project privileged (see the AwsSolutions-CB3 suppression in CDKPipeline.ts, reasoned as 'privileged mode is required to build Lambda functions written in JS/TS'). So the grant is currently aspirational. Resolve one of two ways: expose privileged on CodePipelineEngineProps (or turn it on for the deploy projects, accepting the CB3 nag suppression) and keep the grant, or drop the image-publishing role until container assets are actually supported so the IAM does not overstate what works. Worth deciding alongside the Wave 6 container work (m6-container).

findings.title: The bare-name stage shorthand resolves to an empty region list, so `stages: ['dev']` synthesizes a stage that can never deploy
findings.detail: normalizeStage in v3/config/define.ts gives a stage written as a bare name (or one whose env omits region/regions) an empty regions array. synthTargets then produces zero targets, so `cdk-cicd deploy --stage dev` logs 'nothing to deploy' and exits 0 -- a silent no-op rather than an error or a sensible default. The engine's grantDeployPermissions has to invent a fallback (the pipeline stack's own region) for that case, and its unit test therefore asserts IAM for a configuration that cannot actually deploy, i.e. the fallback branch is unreachable on any real path. The shorthand is prominently documented (`stages: [{...}, 'prod']` in defineCICD's docstring), so this is a real authoring trap, not a corner. Fix direction, in the config layer rather than the engine: either default an omitted region to the deploy-time ambient region (making the shorthand mean 'wherever the creds point', which is what the fallback assumes) or make an empty region list a config error at defineCICD time. Once decided, the engine's fallback and its test either become live or should be deleted.

findings.title: A stage that sets deployRole without cfnExecutionRole has that one role both assumed and passed to CloudFormation, which needs it to be able to pass itself
findings.detail: The forced-role wiring sends a stage's deployRole down two different paths at once. ExecCommand exports it as CDK_CICD_DEPLOY_ROLE_ARN, which resolveSynthesizer turns into DefaultStackSynthesizer.deployRoleArn -- a role the CDK CLI ASSUMES. DeployCommand also passes the same ARN as `cdk deploy --role-arn`, which is CloudFormation's SERVICE role -- a role that is PASSED, not assumed. When a stage configures deployRole and leaves cfnExecutionRole unset, the same role plays both parts, so it must be able to iam:PassRole itself, and nothing in the wrapper arranges or documents that. This is an M3 design wart rather than a defect in the M4 IAM: the engine's sts:AssumeRole grant on the configured deployRole is correct and necessary for the assume path, so it should not be 'fixed' in the other direction. Fix direction: decide whether --role-arn should be driven by cfnExecutionRole only (leaving deployRole purely as the assumed role, which matches the names and the design doc's 'forced deployer / CloudFormation-execution roles' split), and document the trust/PassRole requirement either way. Cheap to get wrong, and only reproducible with a real forced-role stage, which no gate currently exercises.

findings.title: SupportResources provisions on property READ, which is idiomatic in TypeScript but surprising in the other jsii languages
findings.detail: SupportResources implements 'provisioned only when referenced' as getters that create the construct on first access, so reading support.artifactBucket mutates the construct tree. It is jsii-legal (the assembly models both as immutable properties), aws-cdk-lib has precedent for lazily-created children, and the docstrings say 'Created on first read' -- which survives into the generated docs for every language. Still, Python/Java/.NET consumers reasonably assume property access is cheap and idempotent, and a debugger or a REPL inspecting the object would provision resources as a side effect of being looked at. Recorded, not changed, because the alternative (a method like getArtifactBucket()) trades a pleasant call site for honesty and the decision should be made once for the whole support surface rather than per resource -- ideally before the compliance bucket, SSM and VPC members land, and certainly before the v3 major freezes the API. Related, minor: SupportResourcesProps.removalPolicy accepts all five RemovalPolicy values while only DESTROY and RETAIN are meaningful (SNAPSHOT emits a DeletionPolicy CloudFormation rejects for AWS::S3::Bucket) -- consistent with how aws-cdk-lib itself behaves, so probably leave it.

findings.title: The husky pre-commit hook runs eslint --fix across the whole tree, so every commit tends to drag in prettier churn from files the change never touched
findings.detail: The pre-commit hook runs `npm run lint`, which is eslint --fix over all of src/test/build-tools in each package rather than over the staged files. The tree is not currently prettier-clean at HEAD, so the hook rewraps unrelated files (observed on test/v3/config/define.test.ts and test/v3/runtime/synthesizer.test.ts, both pure line-wraps) and leaves them dirty in the working tree. It does not corrupt a commit that stages explicit paths, but it does mean an agent or developer using `git commit -a` silently ships reformatting noise, which directly works against ground rule 5 -- the maintainer reviews the EVOLUTION of the branch, and unrelated churn is exactly what makes that harder. Worked around here by staging explicit paths and reverting the churn. Fix direction (projen-managed, so change projenrc rather than the hook by hand): either make the hook lint only staged files (lint-staged) or run prettier once over the tree in a dedicated style commit so the hook has nothing left to rewrite.

findings.title: The wrapper package resolves a nested second copy of aws-cdk-lib and constructs, which silently disables cdk-nag entirely
findings.detail: Inside packages/@cdklabs/cdk-cicd-wrapper, `require('aws-cdk-lib')` and `require('constructs')` resolve to nested copies under that package's own node_modules, while `cdk-nag` resolves to the hoisted copies at the repo root. Same versions on both sides (aws-cdk-lib 2.195.0, constructs 10.3.0), but they are different module instances -- verified directly: `localCopy === rootCopy` is false for both. Every cdk-nag rule tests resource identity with instanceof against ITS copy of the Cfn* classes, so no rule ever matches and cdk-nag emits NOTHING. Measured, not inferred: a deliberately non-compliant bare s3.Bucket produces zero annotations when synthesized with the package's resolution, and produces AwsSolutions-S1 as expected when both resolve to the same copy. Root cause chain: PipelineConfig.ts declares @cloudcomponents/cdk-pull-request-approval-rule, @cloudcomponents/cdk-pull-request-check and yaml as bundledDeps (required so the jsii package can ship non-jsii runtime deps); projen turns bundled deps into yarn-1 workspaces.nohoist entries of the form `<pkg>/<dep>/**`; the `/**` pulls the whole subtree down, and because those @cloudcomponents packages declare aws-cdk-lib and constructs as PEER dependencies, yarn satisfies the peers with nested installs. Consequences: the package's compliance posture is unverified, and every cdk-nag assertion in its test suite is vacuous (see qa-cdk-nag-compliance-tests-are-vacuous). Note the blast radius is limited to this repo's own test/build resolution -- a user installing the published package has a single aws-cdk-lib, so `applyWrapper`'s AwsSolutionsChecks does fire in their app, which is why this has never shown up as a runtime bug. Confirmed structural rather than a stale-install artifact: the duplication is still present after a full `npx projen` regen + yarn install. Fix direction: narrow or eliminate the nohoist so aws-cdk-lib/constructs stay single-instance (dropping the `/**` suffix, or excluding the peers), then re-measure with the control case above; expect previously-green compliance tests to go red once cdk-nag actually runs. Boundary now measured precisely, because it decides whether the next unit can verify itself: the CLI package resolves aws-cdk-lib from the repo root while the wrapper package resolves its nested copy, so a CLI-hosted pipeline app builds App/Stack from one copy and the engine renders resources from the other. Cross-copy RENDERING is fine -- aws-cdk-lib identity checks such as Stack.of use the global symbol registry, which is shared across copies, and a full render plus synth succeeds -- which is a second reason this never surfaced as a runtime bug. cdk-nag is the part that breaks, because its rules use real instanceof: the same control bucket yields 2 AwsSolutions findings when cdk-nag and the resources share a copy, and 0 across copies. So a pipeline app that applies AwsSolutionsChecks is correct for a published user but its nag pass cannot be verified in this workspace until this is fixed, and any "expect zero findings" assertion written here would be vacuously green.

findings.title: The 'No unsuppressed Warnings/Errors' cdk-nag tests pass unconditionally and assert nothing
findings.detail: The wrapper package's compliance tests assert `expect(findError('*', stringLikeRegexp('AwsSolutions-.*'))).toHaveLength(0)` and similar for warnings. They are green because cdk-nag emits no annotations at all in this package's module resolution (see qa-duplicate-aws-cdk-lib-makes-cdk-nag-inert), not because the stacks are compliant -- so they would stay green no matter how non-compliant the templates became. A second, independent defect makes some of them doubly vacuous: they register the Aspect AFTER `Template.fromStack(stack)` has already synthesized, and the synthesized assembly is cached, so the Aspect would not run on that stack even with correct module resolution. Any assertion shaped 'expect no findings' needs a companion control assertion that the checker is live -- e.g. a throwaway non-compliant resource that MUST produce at least one AwsSolutions finding in the same run -- otherwise a silent false green is indistinguishable from real compliance. Applies to test/stacks/PipelineBlueprintStack.test.ts (the v2 pipeline compliance tests) and should be the pattern for any v3 nag test added later. Fix together with the resolution defect, since fixing resolution alone will turn these red and the failures will be real.

findings.title: The python dependency audit regenerates requirements.txt from a Pipfile and then deletes it, destroying a hand-maintained file
findings.detail: The python branch of the dependency check regenerates a requirements file from a Pipfile so a scanner can read it, then removes it again as cleanup. A project that legitimately keeps BOTH a Pipfile and a hand-maintained requirements file in the same directory therefore loses the hand-maintained one -- an unrecoverable local edit, not just a rebuild. Pre-existing v2 behaviour, but until now it was effectively unreachable: v2's generated task passed no ecosystem flags, so the python path was never enabled by default. `cdk-cicd check` turns `audit` on automatically for any project with a Pipfile, which makes the hazard reachable on a default run. Read from the script rather than executed, so the exact deletion condition should be confirmed before fixing. Fix direction: write the generated file to a temp directory (or a uniquely-named file) and never remove a path the project already had; at minimum refuse to overwrite an existing requirements file.

findings.title: Every cdk-cicd invocation fails at load on a host without python 3, because the security command resolves python at module top level
findings.detail: The security command resolves the python executable in module-scope code, and the CLI entry point imports every command module unconditionally to register it with yargs. So the python probe runs on EVERY `cdk-cicd` invocation, and on a host without python 3 the process dies during module load with 'Python is not installed' -- including for `cdk-cicd --help`, `--version`, `synth` and `deploy`, none of which need python. That makes a python toolchain a hard requirement of the whole CLI rather than of one command, which matters for the v3 story: a plain TypeScript CDK user has no reason to have it, and the deploy CodeBuild image is not guaranteed to. Pre-existing v2 defect, found while wiring `cdk-cicd check`. Fix direction: resolve python lazily inside the handler (or the scanner wrapper), so the failure lands on the command that actually needs it, with a message naming that command.

findings.title: The security check has no skip path, so a runner without python or registry access fails the build instead of degrading
findings.detail: `cdk-cicd check` skips a check whose baseline or manifest is absent, which is a file probe. The `security` check has no such precondition and always runs, but it needs python 3, a writable venv and network access to PyPI plus the semgrep rule registry. On an air-gapped or restricted CI runner it therefore fails the whole `check` run for an environmental reason rather than a code finding, and the failure looks like a security violation. A file probe cannot establish any of those preconditions. Fix direction: probe the toolchain (python present, venv creatable) and skip with a logged reason when it is absent, or expose an explicit opt-out so a restricted runner can declare it; either way keep the distinction between 'scanner could not run' and 'scanner found something' visible in the summary. Consider together with qa-cli-requires-python-at-import, which is the same missing-python condition surfacing far earlier.

findings.title: The check command's yargs handler and child-process spawn are covered only by manual runs, and the entry-point resolution differs between compiled and ts-jest execution
findings.detail: `planChecks` and `runPlans` are unit tested with an injected runner, which is the right seam, but the yargs `handler` and the `spawnCheck` helper around it are exercised only by manual CLI runs against the compiled output. The fragile part is how `spawnCheck` locates the CLI entry to re-invoke: a relative `require.resolve` of the entry module. That is correct for the compiled layout, but it silently depends on the relative depth of the command file, so moving or re-nesting the file breaks the child spawn with no test failure. Worse for testability, under ts-jest the same call resolves to the TypeScript entry, which `node` cannot execute -- so a naive unit test of `spawnCheck` would fail for a reason unrelated to the code being wrong. Fix direction: resolve the entry from the package root (or inject the entry path) so it is assertable, and add a test that pins the resolved target against the compiled layout rather than the test-time one.

findings.title: cdk-cicd check never passes the CI flag to the security scan, so a job switching to it loses the junit report artifacts
findings.detail: v2's CI wiring passed a `--ci` flag to the security scan when a CI environment variable was set, which makes the scanners emit junit-format XML into a reports directory for the build system to collect. `cdk-cicd check` always invokes the scan without that flag, so a project migrating its CI job from the v2 npm scripts to `cdk-cicd check` silently stops producing those report artifacts. No consumer of the reports exists in the wrapper source today, which is why this is low rather than medium -- it matters to whichever task wires the v3 CI step and decides whether the CodeBuild project declares a report group. Fix direction: detect CI the same way v2 did and forward the flag, and if the v3 engine is meant to surface test reports, have the CI project declare the matching report group so the artifacts are actually collected rather than merely written.

findings.title: Configuring any ci.steps REPLACES the default CI commands, so an override silently drops both the check gate and the synth step
findings.detail: The engine builds the CI project's commands as `steps.length > 0 ? ['npm ci', ...steps] : DEFAULT_CI_COMMANDS`. So a project that configures a single extra CI step (say a unit-test command) does not get that step ADDED to the default run -- it gets the whole default run replaced, losing `cdk-cicd check` (validate/audit/license/security) and `cdk-cicd synth --all`. That works directly against what makes those checks default-on: the gate is present only for projects that configured nothing. Nothing fails loudly either, because the deploy actions synth for themselves, so the only symptom is a pipeline that quietly stopped running its own checks. Fix direction: decide and document whether `ci.steps` is additive or a replacement. Additive (append the configured steps after the defaults, with the defaults still first) preserves the gate and is the behaviour the naming implies; if replacement is genuinely wanted, it should be a distinct, explicit opt-out rather than a side-effect of adding one step, and the config type should say so.

findings.title: A yarn-only project gets no dependency audit at all from cdk-cicd check, because the v2 audit command can only drive npm audit
findings.detail: `check`'s audit planner only selects `--npm` for a `package-lock.json`/`npm-shrinkwrap.json` and `--python` for a `Pipfile`, so a project whose lock file is a `yarn.lock` (or whose python deps are a `requirements.txt`) is planned as a skip. The skip is correct given the underlying tool -- v2's audit shells out to `npm audit`, which refuses a yarn-only tree, and the python script only ever resolves Pipfiles -- and skipping is much better than the alternative green run that audited nothing. But the net effect is that a whole class of real projects has NO dependency audit in CI while `cdk-cicd check` reports success, and `validate` still happily checksums the same `yarn.lock` it cannot audit, which makes the gap easy to miss. Fix direction: teach the audit path `yarn npm audit` (yarn 2+) / `yarn audit` (yarn 1) and `pip-audit -r requirements.txt`, so ecosystem coverage follows the project rather than the tool. Until then the skip reason is the only warning a user gets.

findings.title: The security scan builds and then deletes a throwaway python venv per run, so every CI build pays a full cold install of the scanners
findings.detail: v2's scan creates a fresh temp directory, builds a python venv in it, pip-installs its scanners into that venv, and removes the whole directory in a `finally`. Nothing is cached between runs by construction. Interactively that is a sensible hygiene choice; as a default-on CI gate reached through `cdk-cicd check` it means each pipeline build spends minutes on a cold `pip install` of the scanners plus their transitive deps, and takes a hard dependency on registry reachability from inside the build -- a registry blip becomes a red pipeline with a `Security scan failed` message that says nothing about the real cause. Fix direction belongs with whoever sizes the v3 CI project: either point the venv at a cacheable location and declare it in the CodeBuild cache, or bake the scanners into the CI image, so the gate's cost is paid at image-build time instead of on every commit.

findings.title: Each v2 scanner returns `status || 0`, so a scanner killed by a signal reports success
findings.detail: All three scanners end with `return commandResults.status || 0`. `spawnSync` sets `status` to null when the child is terminated by a signal rather than exiting, so an OOM-killed or timed-out scanner -- exactly what a large repo hits on a small CodeBuild container -- yields null, `null || 0` is 0, and the scan reports a clean pass. The same idiom also folds a spawn failure into 0. This is a false green in a security gate, which is what makes it worth fixing even though the trigger is uncommon: the failure mode is silent, and it gets more likely the bigger the scanned tree. Fix direction: `status ?? 1` (with the signal named in the log line), which is the idiom v3's `check` umbrella already uses when it collects a child's exit code. Note that fixing it will surface previously-hidden failures, so it wants to land with the CI sizing work rather than on its own.

findings.title: The license check writes a licensecheck.json into the project root when none exists, so a read-only CI gate mutates the checked-out source tree
findings.detail: v2's license checker loads its config by creating it first: if the configured file is absent it writes a default `licensecheck.json` into the project root, then reads it back. Reached through `cdk-cicd check`, that makes a gate whose job is only to report drift leave a new untracked file in the CI workspace -- harmless in a throwaway checkout, but it means `check` is not side-effect free, it will show up as a dirty tree to any later step that inspects git status, and on a `--fix`-less run the user gets a file they never asked for. Fix direction: treat an absent config as 'use the built-in defaults in memory' and only persist it under `--fix`, matching how the verification file itself is treated. Low because the file is deterministic and the checks still behave correctly with it present.

findings.title: The engine tests assert buildspec contents by regex substring, so they cannot catch a command landing in the wrong phase or the wrong order
findings.detail: The CodePipeline engine tests check what a CodeBuild project runs with `Match.stringLikeRegexp('cdk-cicd check')` against the rendered `Source.BuildSpec`, which is a single JSON string in the template. That confirms the substring appears SOMEWHERE in the buildspec and nothing more: the same assertion passes if the command moves from `build` to `post_build`, if it runs before `npm ci`, or if it ends up in a comment. It also can't express the absence of a command without risking a match on an unrelated one. Fix direction: parse the buildspec string out of the template and assert on the resulting object (`phases.build.commands` as an array), which makes phase and order part of the contract and reads better than a regex. Low because the current assertions are not wrong, just weak -- worth doing when the next change touches these tests.

findings.title: The m4-verify gate has to drive the approval explicitly, or the real pipeline run stalls on it for days
findings.detail: Now that the engine emits real approval gates, any m4-verify fixture stage not named `dev` or `res` is gated by default, so a real pipeline execution reaches that stage and WAITS -- CodePipeline's default approval timeout is 7 days. The deploy never runs, so a gate that asserts a deployed stack would hang rather than fail, and because the pipeline is created with `restartExecutionOnUpdate: true` every subsequent stack update starts another execution that queues behind the pending approval, leaving teardown to run with an execution in flight. Fix direction, and the better test: have the harness prove the gate BOTH ways -- assert the stage stays pending while unapproved, then approve it via `codepipeline put-approval-result` and assert the deploy proceeds. Setting `manualApproval: false` on the fixture stage would also unblock the gate but would leave the approval path itself unproven, which is the more interesting half. This is planning for the gate, not a defect in the engine.

findings.title: A manual approval gate notifies nobody and inherits the 7-day default timeout, with no config surface to change either
findings.detail: The engine emits `ManualApprovalAction` with neither `notifyEmails`/`notificationTopic` nor `timeout`, so nothing tells anyone a gate is waiting and the action fails silently once the CodePipeline default timeout (7 days) elapses. There is no way for a user to configure it either: `StageInput.manualApproval` is a plain boolean. This is v2 parity -- v2's bare `ManualApprovalStep` notified nobody either -- so it is a long-standing gap rather than a regression, and adding a topic now with no user asking for one would be exactly the speculative configurability CLAUDE.md principle 2 rules out. Recorded so the gap is a decision rather than an oversight. Fix direction when a real need appears: widen the stage input to accept an object form (`manualApproval: { notifyEmails, timeout }`) alongside the boolean, rather than bolting notification props onto the engine, so the setting stays with the stage it belongs to.

findings.title: defineCICD never validates stage names, so a bad name surfaces as a raw CDK regex error naming a derived identifier
findings.detail: `normalizeStage` accepts any string as a stage name, so invalid names are caught much later by CDK and reported against an identifier the user never wrote. Reproduced: a 93-character stage name fails with "Action name must match regular expression" quoting the derived `Approve-<name>`; a name containing a space fails on stage-name validation; a stage named `Build` fails as a duplicate stage, because the engine reserves `Source` and `Build`. The 93-character case is a narrow new window opened by the approval work -- the `Approve-` prefix is one character longer than `Deploy-`, so names that previously fit now do not -- while the space and reserved-name cases are pre-existing. All of them fail loudly at synth and none can reach a deploy, which is why this is low. Fix direction: validate in `normalizeStage` that the name matches the CodePipeline-safe pattern with enough headroom for the longest prefix the engine derives, and is not one of the engine's reserved stage names, reporting the stage the user actually wrote.

findings.title: The approval footprint test loops over both gated cases inside one test, so a failure does not say which case broke
findings.detail: The test asserting that gating adds no pipeline stage and no CodeBuild project iterates `for (const gated of [true, false])` inside a single test, so a regression in one case reports the one test name with no indication of which iteration failed; `test.each` would name it. The gated iteration also only asserts what is ABSENT (stage list, project count, topic count) and never that the approval is present, so read alone it would pass an implementation ignoring `manualApproval` entirely -- not a hole in the suite, since a separate test pins the approval and its run order, but it does mean this test is weaker than it looks. Separately, no test renders TWO gated stages at once; distinct action names per gated stage were verified by hand during review rather than pinned. Fix direction: split with `test.each`, add the positive approval assertion to the gated case, and add a two-gated-stage case.

findings.title: PipelineApp uses config.application verbatim as the CloudFormation stackName with no legality check
findings.detail: `PipelineApp` builds `name = `${config.application ?? 'cdk-cicd'}-pipeline`` and uses it as both the construct id and the stack's `stackName`. `defineCICD`/`resolveCicdConfig` sanitize only the qualifier (`deriveQualifier`), never `application`, so an application with dots, spaces, underscores, or long enough to push the stack name past CloudFormation's 128-character limit synthesizes cleanly and then fails late at deploy with a generic CloudFormation validation error rather than a synth-time message naming the field the user set. Sibling to `code-review-stage-name-unvalidated-in-definecicd` (same class of gap, different identifier). Reasoned during review, not executed. Out of scope for m4-approval-selfupdate; validation belongs in `defineCICD` where the application name is first accepted. Fix direction: validate `application` against a CloudFormation-safe pattern in `resolveCicdConfig`, with headroom for the `-pipeline` suffix, reporting the value the user actually wrote.

findings.title: deploy-ci's fail-fast config load only handles undefined, so a THROWN config error surfaces as a raw stack trace
findings.detail: `DeployCiCommand` calls `loadCicdConfig(cwd)` purely to fail fast with a friendly 'no cicd.config.ts' message, but it only branches on the `undefined` return. If `load` instead THROWS -- ts-node not resolvable, or the user's `cicd.config.ts` itself throws at require time -- the error propagates to `index.ts` `main().catch`, which logs `e.stack` and exits 1: a stack trace, not the intended friendly message. This is consistent with the existing `SynthCommand`/`DeployCommand`, which do not catch either, so it is a pre-existing pattern rather than a regression introduced here. Reasoned, not executed. Fix direction (fleet-wide, not just this command): wrap the config load in the v3 commands in one shared helper that turns a throw into a single-line diagnostic.

findings.title: The pipeline-app and deploy-ci command handlers have no unit tests; only the pure argv builders do
findings.detail: Unit tests cover the pure `deployCiArgs`/`pipelineAppCommand` builders and the wrapper-side `PipelineApp`, but neither CLI command's `handler` is exercised: deploy-ci's fail-fast branch, its `spawnSync` call and exit-code propagation, and the whole of `PipelineAppCommand.ts` (no test file at all) rely solely on the m4-verify real-AWS gate. The end-to-end run against the built CLI covered the happy path and the missing-config path by hand during this unit, but nothing pins them in CI. Acknowledged in the test-file comment; acceptable because these handlers are thin spawn shims whose logic lives in the tested builders, but recorded so the gap is a decision. Fix direction: a handler test that injects a fake spawn and asserts argv + exit code, mirroring how the deploy handler could be tested.

findings.title: PipelineApp is exported to all jsii languages but its required config can only be built by the TS-only defineCICD
findings.detail: `PipelineApp`/`PipelineAppProps` are exported from the v3 barrel and cross the jsii boundary (subclassing `aws-cdk-lib.App` is jsii-sound and `PipelineAppProps` is a proper readonly struct). But `PipelineAppProps.config: ResolvedCicdConfig` can in practice only be produced by `defineCICD`, a free function with a union-typed input that jsii omits (see the barrel comment and design open-question O1). So the advertised 'explicit opt-in: instantiate PipelineApp in your own bin/' story holds only for TypeScript consumers; a Python/Java consumer can import `PipelineApp` but has no ergonomic way to construct a `ResolvedCicdConfig` to pass it. Not a defect in this unit -- it is the same non-TS authoring gap O1 already tracks, now reachable through a second door -- but worth recording against PipelineApp specifically. Fix direction is whatever O1 lands (a jsii-modeled config builder); until then the non-TS opt-in path is provisioning via `cdk-cicd deploy-ci`, not `new PipelineApp`.
